# Cognitive Load

The amount of mental effort a task asks of a person while they use an interface: what they must remember, compare, decide and interpret at once. Designers usually mean the extra load the interface adds on top of the task itself, which is the part we can remove.

## In Practice

- Fewer things to hold in memory: show the selected seat, the payee or the amount on the screen where the decision happens, not three steps back.
- One decision per step when the decision is consequential, such as confirming a transfer.
- Familiar patterns over clever ones. Every new pattern costs a moment of learning.
- Plain labels. A term the user has to translate is load.
- Time pressure multiplies everything else. A countdown with no warning turns a simple choice into a stressful one.

## Where I Have Seen It

The Copperline transfer flow got easier mostly by removing choices, not by adding help text ([[copperline-usability-test-2026-05-21]]). The Tallowmere seat hold is the opposite case: a small choice made hard by a hidden timer ([[tallowmere-seat-map-findings]]). Think-aloud sessions are where it shows up most clearly, as long pauses and people reading the same line twice ([[think-aloud-testing]]).

## Caveats

It is a useful way to talk about design decisions with clients, less useful as a measurement. I do not measure it directly; task time, errors and SUS scores are the evidence I use.
